questions.q: Why does a pending-approval store that works fine as a local Python dict break once the agent is deployed?
options: Python dicts are not supported inside containers
A deployed service restarts, redeploys, and often runs multiple instances, so an in-memory dict loses pending requests that haven't yet been resolved
Dicts cannot hold JSON-shaped data
Deployment automatically converts all variables to strings
questions.explain: In-memory state only survives as long as the process does. A real deployment's restarts and multiple instances mean a pending approval recorded only in memory can vanish before a reviewer ever acts on it.

questions.q: Where do secrets like ANTHROPIC_API_KEY and database credentials belong in the Dockerfile shown in this lesson?
options: Hardcoded directly in the Dockerfile with an ENV instruction set to the real value
They don't appear in the Dockerfile at all -- they're passed as environment variables at container runtime
Inside requirements.txt
In a comment at the top of the Dockerfile
questions.explain: The Dockerfile intentionally contains no secret values. Credentials are supplied when the container actually runs, so they're never baked into an image that anyone with a copy of it could read.

questions.q: What specifically breaks if audit log entries are only written to stdout in a deployed container?
options: Nothing -- stdout is always permanently preserved
Container logs are often rotated or lost on redeploy, so an audit trail that depends only on stdout isn't durable enough to answer later questions
stdout cannot hold JSON-formatted text
The agent will crash immediately on startup
questions.explain: stdout-only logs are ephemeral in most deployment setups -- the audit log needs to land in durable storage (a database or shipped log pipeline) to actually serve its purpose after a redeploy or rotation.

questions.q: What does this lesson say stays the same, and what changes, when Lessons 14-16's logic moves from a local script to a deployed service?
options: The tool schemas and approval logic all have to be rewritten
The logic itself doesn't change; where its state (pending approvals, audit logs) lives has to change from in-process memory to durable storage
Validation becomes unnecessary once deployed
The approval workflow only works locally and cannot be deployed
questions.explain: The approval, validation, and logging logic from earlier lessons carries over unchanged -- what has to change is making sure the state that logic depends on can survive restarts and multiple instances.

questions.q: Which existing course does this lesson say its Dockerfile and secrets-handling pattern directly applies?
options: The Tableau course
The Docker & Deployment for AI Applications course
The Snowflake course
The PowerShell Fundamentals course
questions.explain: This lesson explicitly applies the Docker & Deployment for AI Applications course's Dockerfile and environment-variable-secrets material directly, rather than introducing new deployment concepts.
